name: Cetrimonium chloride

lead: Cetrimonium chloride is a positively charged surfactant found in many conditioners, usually paired with fatty alcohols. It softens hair and reduces static.
It is an ingredient rather than a treatment, and no hair-appearance trials were found.

paras: The positively charged head binds to negatively charged hair; with fatty alcohols and water it forms a creamy lamellar gel.
Dermatology reviews list it among quaternary ammonium compounds linked to contact dermatitis. Concentrated forms are corrosive and toxic to aquatic life, per Grokipedia.

lead: Cetrimonium chloride (cetyltrimethylammonium chloride, CTAC) is a quaternary ammonium cationic surfactant, formula C19H42ClN, used in hair conditioners and shampoos and also as an antiseptic.[1][2] In conditioners it is typically combined with long-chain fatty alcohols such as stearyl alcohol; the mixture forms a lamellar gel with water. Cationic surfactant levels are typically about 1 to 2 percent.[1]

Grokipedia reports that the Cosmetic Ingredient Review panel considered it safe in rinse-off products and at up to 0.25 percent in leave-on products when formulated to limit irritation.[2] Dermatology literature lists it among quaternary ammonium compounds reported as contact allergens or irritants.[3]

paras: Beyond hair conditioners, it is classed as a topical antiseptic and surfactant (ATC codes D08AJ02 and R02AA17).[1] Grokipedia also lists industrial biocide and phase-transfer catalyst roles.[2]
An analytical study described methods for measuring it and fatty alcohols in hair conditioners.[4]

A 2023 review of quaternary ammonium compounds and contact dermatitis lists cetrimonium chloride among those identified as potential culprits of skin reactions, with use rising during the COVID-19 pandemic.[3] Patch-test surveillance papers also include quaternary surfactants.[5] Grokipedia reports that the concentrated substance is classed as causing severe skin burns and eye damage and as very toxic to aquatic life.[2]
Animal studies of ophthalmic preservatives, including cetrimonium chloride, have examined effects on the conjunctiva; these concern eye drops, not hair products.[6]
No studies found of its effect on hair appearance. Related literature includes contact-dermatitis reviews and patch-test studies of quaternary ammonium compounds.[3][5]
